why: The student wrote a correct index loop that writes each product back into a[i]. This fixes the given code's failing for-each loop, which only changed the copy x. Fixing one given failing case with a familiar canonical traversal is L3, not L4.

concepts.quote: for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) a[i] = a[i] * 10;
concepts.why: The loop variable is used as the index, so a[i] reaches and updates a different element on each pass. The run turns [5,4,3,2,1] into [50,40,30,20,10].
It reads and writes each element through the loop index, so the same expression a[i] reaches every position in turn.
a.length is used correctly, without parentheses, as the loop bound, so the loop fits the array's real size instead of a hard-coded number.
The answer doesn't use or say anything about the for-each loop. Avoiding it is only an implicit fix, not a claim about the concept.
